Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining the second panel. Before we start, a word about the format, because it is a little different this year. Each panelist will see one real clause on the screen, from a contract or a regulation in their country. They will have sixty seconds to explain it. One request to our panelists: please do not read the clause aloud. The audience can read it on the screen, and most of them read faster than we speak. Tell us what it means. Who has to do what, and what happens if they do not. Our audience today is mostly investors and engineers, not lawyers, so imagine you are explaining it to a smart friend over coffee. After the sixty seconds, the floor is open for questions.

When I was at the agency, we had a simple test before we published any new rule. We gave the draft to one person outside the agency, an engineer or a journalist, and we asked them to explain the rule back to us in one minute. If they could not, the rule was not ready. Not the law, the words. Over the years I learned that every explanation has to answer three questions. Who has to do what. By when. And what happens if they do not. People sometimes say that plain language means simple law. It does not. The rule stays exactly as precise as before, with every condition and every exception. Only the words change. Shall becomes has to. Notwithstanding becomes even if. And suddenly the people who have to follow the rule can actually understand it.
